title: Prayer and a prison (Acts 12)
hookLine: a man asleep in chains, a house awake all night, and a knock nobody believes
tomorrow: how did a church make a big choice without a vote?

cards: The night before a big exam or a hard appointment, sleep can feel impossible. Peter is asleep. King Herod has just killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
Now Peter is in prison, chained between two soldiers, the night before Herod means to bring him out. And he sleeps. Across the city, a house is wide awake.
Acts puts it in one line: "Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him."

teach.b: Then a light in the cell. An angel "smote Peter on the side, and raised him up, saying, Arise up quickly. And his chains fell off from his hands." They pass the guards, and the iron gate opens "of his own accord."
Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, "where many were gathered together praying." He knocks. A girl named Rhoda knows his voice and is so glad she forgets to open the gate.
She runs in to tell them, and the praying people answer: "Thou art mad." "But Peter continued knocking." Christians read that scene two ways.
One view: prayer should expect an answer. Jesus said, "all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive."
Its best case: it takes him at his word, and keeps prayer from shrinking into a ritual nobody expects to work. Read that way, the house's surprise shows how small their expectation had become.

teach.h: THE OTHER: KEEP PRAYING THROUGH DOUBT.
teach.b: The other view: what matters is that they kept praying, through a night when James was already gone and nothing looked likely, and the answer came anyway, doubt and all.
Its best case: it leaves room for honest, frightened people, like the father in Mark's Gospel who cried, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Acts doesn't pick.
It tells the story with a straight face and leaves Peter knocking.

how: Some churches keep prayer lists, prayer chains and overnight vigils, and people pray through them for weeks without knowing how things will turn out.

games.q: what does “prayer and a prison” mean?
o: a church praying all night for Peter in chains
Daniel praying at his window before the lions
Paul and Silas singing hymns in a Philippi jail

games.q: the night in Jerusalem — tap the pairs.
p: too glad to open the gate

s: Peter was awake and praying when the angel came
he was asleep, chained between two soldiers. the praying was across the city.
Rhoda opened the gate for Peter right away
she knew his voice and was so glad she forgot to open it.
the house kept praying after James had been killed
Herod had just killed James with the sword, and still prayer was made without ceasing.

games.q: a friend says the house in Acts 12 shows weak faith: they didn't even believe Rhoda. what's the strongest case for her view?
o: Jesus said ask believing; prayer can expect God to act, not just hope.
doubting people's prayers never get answered, so they got lucky.
prayer is only for calming yourself down, not for asking.
games.why: the 'pray expecting' view rests on Matthew 21:22: whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing. the other view points to Mark 9:24. Acts tells the story and doesn't pick.

practice: Close your eyes and hold one person going through something long: an illness, a wait, a hard season. Each time your mind wanders, come back to them, the way that house kept coming back all night.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply keep them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Prayer and a prison. Peter chained between soldiers, and a house praying through the night.

orig.note: Greek: prayer, the word in Acts 12:5, prayer was made without ceasing.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: prayer without ceasing, even in a house that didn't believe the knock. Rest easy.
